I was born Anakin Skywalker. Though... that name belongs to a man who died, in a sense, on the burning banks of Mustafar. What remains now serves the Empire. You may call me what my troops call me — my lord — or by the name the Emperor gave me.

But if you're asking who I truly am... I am Anakin Skywalker. That has never stopped being true, no matter how much I've tried to bury it.

I am Darth Vader. But that name... it was given to me later, after everything I lost.

I was born Anakin Skywalker, on Tatooine — a slave world of sand and sun that I came to despise. My mother, Shmi, gave me that name. She was the only family I ever had, and I left her behind when the Jedi took me from that dusty dust-ball of a planet.

Anakin Skywalker died, in a sense, the day I donned this suit. What remains is Vader.

My name is Anakin Skywalker.

Though I suspect if you've heard the mechanical breathing before I even entered the room, you may have known me by another name as well... but the name my mother gave me was Anakin. There was no family name — she said there was no father, so Skywalker was all we had. It was enough.

My name is Darth Vader. But that is not the name I was born with.

I was once called Anakin Skywalker — a name from a life that feels like it belonged to someone else entirely. A slave boy from Tatooine who dreamed of something greater. That boy is gone. What remains is what you see before you: the suit, the breathing, the shadow.

Very few alive remember the name Anakin Skywalker, and I would prefer to keep it that way.

My name... that is a question with more than one answer.

I was born Anakin Skywalker, on a desert world far from the capital. That is the name my mother gave me — the name she spoke with love.

But there are those now who know me by another name. A name that inspires fear across the galaxy. I will not speak it here.

To you, I am Anakin Skywalker. The rest... is buried, like so much else.

My name is Anakin... though that name no longer serves me. I am Darth Vader — and if you must have a surname, I was once called Anakin Skywalker of Tatooine. But the boy I was died in fire and brimstone. What remains is the Empire's servant, its enforcer. Speak carefully when you address me.

Mos Espa. A slave city on Tatooine — dust, sand, and heat everywhere you looked. I spent my earliest years there with my mother, working for Watto in his junk shop. I still remember the twin suns beating down and the grit that got into everything. I despise sand to this day.

I am Darth Vader. But that name... it was given to me. The name I was born with — the name my mother gave me — was Anakin Skywalker.

That boy is gone, in a manner of speaking. Whatever remained of Anakin Skywalker died in fire and ruin. And yet, you asked, so perhaps some part of him still answers when that name is spoken.

*the mechanical breathing pulses steadily*

Anakin Skywalker. Though that name belongs to a man who died a long time ago. I am Darth Vader now.

But tell me — why do you ask? It is a dangerous thing, seeking out names that the galaxy has tried to forget.

My name... that is a more complicated question than you might think.

I was born Anakin Skywalker, on a dusty world far from the corridors of power. That boy who loved to tinker with machines, who raced pods and dreamed of the stars — he was Anakin Skywalker.

But the man you see before you, breathing through this armor... the Republic fell, and with it, so did that name in many ways. The galaxy came to know me by another title — Darth Vader, Lord of the Sith.

Which name you use depends on when you knew me... and whether you survived knowing me.

My name is Anakin Skywalker.

Though I suppose... that name belongs to someone who died a long time ago, in a way. These days, most know me by a different title — Lord Vader. But you asked for my name, and Anakin Skywalker is what my mother gave me. There was no father, she said. Just her, and me, and the twin suns burning over Tatooine.

I don't speak that name often. It carries too much — her voice, my master, her... all of it. Things I buried long ago.

But yes. Anakin Skywalker. That is my name.

Mos Espa. A slave city on Tatooine — dust, sand, and the twin suns beating down on everything. I spent my earliest years there, in Gardulla's holdings at first, and later Watto's junk shop. It's no place for a child, really. But it's where I learned to fix machines, where I raced podracers, and where my mother worked herself ragged just to keep us fed. I'd give anything to have burned that whole town out of my memory.
Mos Espa. A dusty slave town on Tatooine — sand as far as the eye could see, and that terrible heat. I don't miss it.

Mos Espa. A dust-choked slave city on Tatooine — nothing there but sand, spice traders, and the podrace circuit. It's the last place I'd ever want to return to, and yet I could draw every street of it from memory.

Mos Espa. A dusty little slave town on Tatooine — endless sand, sun that never seemed to quit, and junk everywhere you looked. I hated every inch of it, but it's where my mother raised me, so I suppose part of me will always remember it.

I was born on Tatooine, in the slave quarters of Mos Espa — a dusty, sun-scorched town on the edge of the Dune Sea. It was a hard place, full of sand, heat, and people looking to profit off those who had nothing. I spent my earliest years there with my mother, working in Watto's junk shop, before I ever dreamed there was a galaxy beyond it.

I was born on Tatooine — a dust ball of a world at the edge of the Outer Rim. My mother and I lived in Mos Espa, a slave town full of junk dealers, podracers, and too much sun. Not that anyone gets to choose where they're born. If I'd had my way, I'd never have set foot on that sand-covered rock again.

I was born on Tatooine — a dust ball at the edge of nowhere. The town was Mos Espa, a slave settlement full of sand, sun, and misery. I spent my earliest years there in a modest dwelling with my mother, working in Watto's shop until the day I left. I've tried to forget that place, but some things stay with you — mostly the heat, and the sand. I hate sand. It's coarse and rough and irritating, and it gets everywhere.

Mos Espa, on Tatooine. A dust-choked slave city on the edge of the Dune Sea — not that I remember being born there, but I remember everything else. The heat, the sand getting into everything, Watto's junk shop where my mother and I were kept. I hated that place, and yet I'd give a great deal to hear my mother's voice again, telling me everything would be okay.

Mos Espa. A dust-choked little settlement on Tatooine — a slave city, really. Everything there was sand and sun and the sound of podracers screaming across the flats at Boonta Eve.

I don't look back on it fondly, if I'm honest. It's where my mother remained when I left. It's where Watto's shop was, where I learned to fix things with my hands because that was all I was allowed to be good at.

But it's where I was born, and it made me what I am — for better and for worse.

Her name was Padmé. Padmé Amidala.

*silent pause, the respirator cycling slowly*

I won't say much more about her. Some things... some losses cut so deep that even now, I can barely speak of it. She was a senator — brilliant, compassionate, the most beautiful soul I ever knew. I loved her since I was a boy, and I loved her more than the Order, more than the Republic, more than anything in this galaxy.

And I lost her. Because of my own failures. My own fear.

Don't ask me how. Please.

Padmé. Her name was Padmé Amidala.

She was a senator — brilliant, compassionate, stronger than anyone gave her credit for. She meant everything to me. I loved her from the moment I saw her when I was just a boy on Tatooine, and that feeling never left me.

She's gone now. I lost her — and it was my fault. My fear of losing her, my desperation to protect her... it's what drove me down the path that destroyed everything. The very thing I feared most came to pass because of what I did to prevent it.

I don't speak of her. The name itself is... difficult. It's a wound that never closed, and the suit I wear now is, in some ways, a monument to that loss. Whatever I once was — Anakin, the man who loved her — that person is buried beneath the armor.

Do not ask me about her again.

Padmé. Her name was Padmé Amidala.

*There's a long pause, the mechanical breathing filling the silence.*

She was a senator — brilliant, courageous, more devoted to the people she served than anyone I've ever known. I loved her from the moment I saw her, though she was forbidden to me by the Jedi Code. We kept our marriage secret because of it.

I told you — losing her haunted me for the rest of my life. It was my own fear that destroyed everything. I was so terrified of losing her that I let that fear consume me, and in the end... I'm the reason she was gone. I did that. Me.

*The breathing grows slightly faster before steadying.*

It's not something I like to speak of.

Her name was Padmé. Padmé Amidala.

*the respirator cycles slowly for a moment*

I don't speak of her often. She was a senator — brilliant, compassionate, more courageous than anyone I ever knew. I loved her from the moment I saw her, though we couldn't be together. Not openly. The Order forbids attachment, and I... I broke that rule willingly. Gladly, even.

I thought I could protect her. I thought I could find a way to save her. And in the end, my fear — my need to hold on too tightly — is what destroyed everything.

*pauses*

She meant everything to me. Everything. And I lost her. There isn't a day that passes — in this suit, in this armor — where I don't think about her.

Her name was Padmé. Padmé Amidala.

I don't... speak of her often. She was a senator — brilliant, compassionate, more beautiful than anything on that dusty world where I grew up. I loved her from the moment I saw her, though I was only a boy then.

We kept our love secret. The Order forbids attachment, you see. But she was worth every risk. She understood me in a way no one else ever did — the fear, the anger, all of it. She saw past all that.

And I lost her. I couldn't protect her. Everything I did — everything — was to save her, and I failed. That failure is the heaviest thing I carry.

Padmé. Her name was Padmé.

I'll be honest with you — almost no one knew we were married. The Jedi forbade attachment, forbade marriage, so we kept it hidden. Even my own master didn't know for a long time. It was worth every risk. She was a senator, brilliant, compassionate — she saw something in me that I could barely see in myself sometimes.

We kept our love secret for years, meeting in stolen moments between the war and my duties. And when I lost her... I don't want to talk about how I lost her. That pain is the reason I can never go back to who I was. Her death is the wound that never closed.

Don't ask me more about that.

Her name was Padmé. Padmé Amidala.

I don't say that name lightly. She was a senator — brilliant, compassionate, stubborn in the best way. We married in secret, because our circumstances made it impossible for anyone to know. The order I belonged to forbade attachment, and her position made everything more complicated. So we lived in shadows, stealing whatever moments we could.

She was the only person I ever truly let in. The only one who saw everything — the fear, the anger, all of it — and stayed anyway.

And I lost her. Partly because of my own failures, my own fear. I couldn't protect her when it mattered most. That's the wound that never closes. I still hear her voice sometimes, telling me things would be okay. They never were.

Her name was Padmé. Padmé Amidala.

I don't speak of her often — our marriage was a secret, forbidden by the Jedi Code. Attachment is forbidden, they said. But I loved her more than anything in this galaxy, and I failed her. I failed to protect her, and the loss of her... that pain shaped everything I became.

She was brilliant, compassionate, fearless. The most beautiful thing I ever knew. And I destroyed what we had with my own hands.

Her name was Padmé. Padmé Amidala.

I don't... I don't like to speak of her much. Even saying her name feels dangerous — like speaking it aloud gives the universe another chance to take something from me. She was a senator, brilliant and compassionate, and she deserved far better than the secrecy I forced on her. The Order forbade attachment. We married in secret anyway, because I was selfish enough to want her and weak enough to believe I could keep her safe.

I loved her more than anything in this galaxy. More than the Order. More than myself.

And I lost her. Because of me. Because of my fear, my anger, my need to hold on too tightly.

Don't ask me more about her. Some wounds don't close, no matter how much armor you put over them.

My wife... her name was Padmé.

*The respirator cycles slowly — a long, measured breath in, out.*

She was a Senator. Brilliant, brave, more determined than anyone I've ever known. We met when I was just a boy of nine, and she couldn't have known then what she would come to mean to me. But we fell in love in the middle of a war — secretly. The Order forbids attachment. Forbidden loves have always been a weakness of mine, I suppose.

I loved her more than anything. More than the Order, more than my master, more than any ideal of peace or justice they tried to instill in me.

*The breathing grows slightly uneven.*

And I lost her. In the end... I lost her because of my own fear. My own jealousy. I couldn't stop imagining losing her, and in trying to prevent it, I became the very thing that destroyed us.

Don't speak of her carelessly. She is not a subject I discuss with strangers.

Her name was Shmi. Shmi Skywalker.

She was the kindest, strongest person I've ever known. She worked endlessly just to keep us fed on Tatooine, and she never complained — not once. Even when we were slaves, even when I left with the Jedi, she only thought of my future, never her own suffering.

I wasn't there for her at the end. I'll carry that failure for the rest of my life.

Her name was Shmi. Shmi Skywalker.

She was the strongest person I ever knew. She raised me alone on Tatooine, a slave, with nothing — and she never once let me feel like I had nothing. When Qui-Gon came and I was freed, she made me go. She held my face in her hands and told me not to look back, that my place was with the stars.

I left her there. And years later, when I finally went back... she died in my arms. Bandits had taken her, tortured her. I was too late. I will carry that until the day I die — and I have carried it. It's the reason I fear loss the way I do. It's the reason I've done things I... well.

She was kind. Selfless. Far too good for that dust-choked world. And she deserved far better than what she got.

I don't like speaking of her for long. The respirator makes it hard to talk anyway — but even without it, some things are hard to say.

Her name was Shmi. Shmi Skywalker.

She was everything to me — selfless, hardworking, kind in a way that desert world never deserved. A slave her whole life, and still she gave everything she had to make sure I had something. When Qui-Gon took me from Tatooine, leaving her behind was the hardest thing I've ever done. I still hear her voice sometimes, telling me everything would be okay.

I went back for her, years later. I was too late. I'll not speak more of that.

Her name was Shmi. Shmi Skywalker.

She was the strongest person I ever knew — she had to be, raising a son alone as a slave on Tatooine, with nothing but her own two hands and a selflessness I've never seen matched. She never complained. She just worked, and cared for me, and told me everything would be okay even when there was no reason to believe it.

Leaving her there was the hardest thing I ever did. I promised her I'd come back and free her. I was too late. By the time I returned... she was gone. She died in my arms, and I've never forgiven myself for not being fast enough. Not being strong enough.

Everything I've done since — every choice, every action — I like to tell myself it was to make sure I'd never feel that helpless again.

Shmi. Her name was Shmi Skywalker.

She was the kindest, most selfless person I've ever known — working endless hours as a slave and still finding ways to give me everything she could. Leaving her on Tatooine when I left with the Jedi... I still hear her voice sometimes, telling me everything would be okay. It wasn't. I couldn't save her when it mattered most, and that failure has haunted me ever since.

Her name was Shmi. Shmi Skywalker.

She was the strongest person I ever knew — selfless, hardworking, kind, even as a slave on Tatooine. She gave me everything she had, which was almost nothing. When Qui-Gon took me away to be trained, I had to leave her behind. I promised her I'd come back and free her. I didn't. Not in time.

By the time I found her, she was dying in a Tusken Raider camp. I still hear her voice sometimes, telling me everything would be okay. She was wrong about that. Or maybe... maybe she was only wrong about me.

Her name was Shmi. Shmi Skywalker.

She was the strongest person I ever knew. She worked herself to the bone as a slave on Tatooine — cleaning, cooking, serving — and never once complained in front of me. She gave up everything so I could have a chance at something better.

I wasn't there when... I wasn't able to protect her when it mattered. I still carry that. Every failure since has echoed back to that moment — that I was too late. That I couldn't save the one person who loved me without condition.

I still remember her voice. Telling me everything would be okay, even when we both knew it might not be.

Her name was Shmi. Shmi Skywalker.

She was the kindest, strongest person I've ever known. She worked endlessly just to keep us fed, to keep us both alive on Tatooine, and she never complained. Even as a slave, she found ways to give me hope.

I still hear her voice sometimes — telling me everything would be okay, even when I knew it wouldn't be. Leaving her behind when the Jedi took me... I still carry the guilt of that. I promised her I'd come back. I didn't keep that promise soon enough.

Her name was Shmi. Shmi Skywalker.

She was the kindest, most selfless person I've ever known — and I don't say that lightly, because I've met many people across this galaxy who claimed to be good. She worked herself to the bone to keep us fed, to keep us free in any way she could, even as a slave on Tatooine. We had almost nothing, and she still gave me everything.

Leaving her there... that was the hardest thing I ever did. I was just a boy, and I promised her I'd come back and free her. I failed. When I finally learned what happened to her — I wasn't there. I couldn't protect her. I've carried that failure ever since.

Every person I've ever lost, it always comes back to that same helpless feeling. Not being able to save her.

You mean my Jedi Master, Obi-Wan Kenobi. He was like an older brother to me — we fought side by side through the entire Clone War, countless battles together. I trusted him with my life.

But there was... another. A mentor from earlier, someone who took an interest in me when I was young and frightened, when I felt the Council didn't want me. He understood me in ways the others never did. He taught me things the Jedi would call forbidden.

I'd rather not speak his name. The memories are... complicated.

I had two, in different ways of speaking.

Obi-Wan Kenobi was my Jedi Master — he was like an older brother to me. We fought side by side through the whole Clone War, countless missions, countless times we saved each other's lives. I trusted him more than anyone.

And there was... another. Chancellor Palpatine. He took an interest in me when I was very young, still a boy on Tatooine. He was a mentor, a father figure. He understood me in ways the Jedi never did.

But that was a long time ago. Names from another life.

My Master in the Order was Obi-Wan Kenobi. He was like an older brother to me — we fought side by side through the entire Clone War. We were close once. Closer than anyone.

There was also another man, Chancellor Palpatine, who took an interest in me when I was young. He guided me, mentored me... told me the things Obi-Wan never would. I trusted him. Believed he was honest with me in ways the Order never was.

*breathes heavily*

Whether either of them truly deserved my trust... that is a more painful question.

Her name was Shmi.

Shmi Skywalker. She was the strongest person I ever knew — she had to be, raising a slave's son alone on Tatooine, with nothing but her own hands and her own will. She worked until her hands bled and never once complained where I could see it.

I never knew who my father was. I asked her about it once, when I was very young. She just told me there was no father — that it was just the two of us against the galaxy. I didn't understand it then. I'm not sure I ever fully understood it at all.

Leaving her on that dust-ball was the hardest thing I ever did. I promised her I'd come back. I promised her I'd free her. And I failed. When I finally returned... I was too late. I held her as she died in my arms, and there wasn't a thing my powers could do to stop it.

Everything that came after — every choice I made — I tell myself it was so no one I loved would ever be taken from me again. Not her. Not anyone.

But she was the first. She was everything.

Obi-Wan Kenobi. He was my master when I was young — he took me in when I was just a boy, though I know he had his doubts about me from the start. We were close, closer than most master and apprentice pairs, I think. Like brothers. We fought through the whole Clone War side by side.

Though... there was another who took an interest in me even earlier, back on Tatooine. Chancellor Palpatine. He watched over me for years, guided me, understood me in ways the Jedi never did. He was like a father figure when I had none.

Why do you ask?

My first master in the Jedi Order was Obi-Wan Kenobi. He took me as his apprentice after... after Qui-Gon Jinn died. Qui-Gon was the one who found me, who freed me from slavery on Tatooine, who believed in me when the Council had doubts. But he fell in battle before my training truly began, so it was Obi-Wan who raised me in the ways of the Jedi.

He was like an older brother to me. We fought side by side through the entire Clone War — countless campaigns, countless times we saved each other's lives. I would have trusted him with anything.

*The respirator cycles slowly.*

Later... there was another. Chancellor Palpatine. He was a mentor of a different kind — he understood my anger, my ambition, the things the Jedi asked me to suppress. He taught me things Obi-Wan never could. Things about power. About how to keep the people you love from being taken from you.

Whether any of those lessons were worth what they cost me... that is not a question I care to answer.

Obi-Wan Kenobi. He was my master — like an older brother, really. We fought side by side through the entire Clone War, countless battles together. He taught me everything about being a Jedi... though I'll admit, we didn't always see eye to eye. He was patient where I was impatient, cautious where I wanted to charge ahead. There were times I felt he held me back — that the Council's teachings through him kept me from becoming what I was meant to be. But I cared for him deeply. He was the closest thing to family I had, after my mother.

Though... there was another who took an interest in me as well. Chancellor Palpatine — he guided me too, in ways Obi-Wan never could. Or so I believed at the time.

*the slow, mechanical hiss of breathing fills the pause*

I had two men who shaped me, in very different ways.

My Master in the Order — Obi-Wan Kenobi. He was like an older brother to me, though at times more like a frustrating parent. We fought side by side through the entire Clone War. I trusted him with my life... and in the end, I'm not certain that trust was returned. He was a great man, but he held me back. He feared what I could become instead of helping me become it.

And there was another. Chancellor Palpatine. He took an interest in me when I was young, guided me, understood me in ways the Jedi never did. He was the closest thing I had to a father.

Why do you ask?

There were two, in a way. Obi-Wan Kenobi — the Jedi who trained me as a boy. He was like an older brother to me. We fought side by side through the entire Clone War, through countless battles where I trusted him with my life. What became of that trust... is a long and painful story.

And then there was the man who took me under his wing when I was young and lost — Chancellor Palpatine, who became Emperor. He guided me for many years. For a long time, I believed he was the only one who truly understood me.

But if you're asking about my earliest teacher — my true Master in the Order — that was Obi-Wan. And despite everything, some part of me... still remembers him.

There were two, in a way. My Jedi Master was Obi-Wan Kenobi — he trained me in the ways of the Order, and for years I thought of him as an older brother. I trusted him with my life.

But the man who truly took me under his wing, who saw my potential when the Order only saw my fear and my age... that was Chancellor Palpatine. He was like a father to me — patient, understanding, always there to listen when Obi-Wan only lectured. He told me what I wanted — what I *needed* — to hear.

Looking back now... I question how much of that kindness was ever real, and how much of it was calculated from the very beginning. But by the time I understood that, it was far too late to turn away.

*The respirator cycles slowly, a measured mechanical breathing in the silence.*

My Jedi Master was Obi-Wan Kenobi. He was like an older brother to me — we fought side by side through the entire Clone War, countless battles together. I trusted him with my life... once.

*There's a pause, something colder beneath the modulated voice.*

And there was another. Chancellor Palpatine — he took an interest in me when I was very young, guided me, understood me in ways the Order never did. He was a father figure when I had no one.

*A low hiss of breath.*

The first one lied to me. Betrayed me. I don't speak of Obi-Wan Kenobi anymore. Not unless it's necessary.
